name: 4 - Defining Problems with the Public
content:
WEBVTT
 
 Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS): Okay, so now I will open the waiting room, and we will wait, like, 3 more minutes to start, and I will… Okay, so I will open it. I will disappear, give me a moment to disappear.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Nice.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Welcome, everyone. If you're just joining us, bear with us. We're going to give it a few minutes to let people in from the waiting room.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And we'll get started in just a moment.
 
 Mauricio Ribeiro: Oh.
 
 Mauricio Ribeiro: Similar work to me.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: As you're coming in, let me just encourage you to please mute yourself,
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And, to pass the time while we let people in from the waiting room, we've put up a short three-question anonymous survey, so we'll just ask you to take that.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And I'll make some announcements in just a moment, but we're just letting people in.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Thank you.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: I think what we'll do in the interest of time, we have a lot of people joining us, but I'll go ahead with some administrative announcements, and that will leave us maximum time for our speaker and our conversation. So let me get us started as people come in from the waiting room.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Again, if you're just joining us, please feel free to go ahead and rename yourself by right-clicking on your square.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: We'd love to know who's here. You can add anything you want, your affiliation, your organization, your agency, pronouns as you prefer.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Please also make sure that you're on mute, and go ahead and take the short three-question anonymous survey, which you'll see in front of you. It just asks you three questions about what you're hoping to learn, and we simply use this to develop our future programming.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Thank you to everybody for being with us today. This is the fourth in our series on AI and public engagement, our Reboot Democracy series. This is a collaboration between Innovate US, the Gov Lab, the Allen Lab for Democratic Renovation at Harvard.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: and Professor Daniel Allen. And we're very, very happy today, to have with us Claudius Levin. Claudius is a political scientist and urban development expert, and most importantly, for our purposes today, director of the DPUS program.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: That is using AI in exciting and innovative ways to help citizens speak, and more importantly, cities listen to what they have to say.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: He has been with the Hamburg Ministry of Urban Development and Housing since 2008, where he's led a lot of innovative programs that I hope we're going to hear more about today.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And unusually today, let me just add one more administrative announcement, Claudius, before I pass the mic to you, is we are experimenting with AI-enabled real-time translation.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So, you can, we're gonna post the instructions for that in the chat. You need to just choose English as the spoken language, as the original language.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And then you can click on your preferred language if you would like it to be in German, or in Spanish, or in something else. Agata, anything else I need to say on the translation before we get started?
 
 Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS): No, I already passed the information on how to turn on the closed captions in the chat, so if anyone has a question, please reach me through chat, and I will be happy to answer.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Okay, I'm gonna end the poll, and
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So we can get our screens back. And… Claudius, let me pass it to you. We're eager to hear from you.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: about the work that you have been doing building open source analytics to help government agencies to listen, and we just want to welcome everybody, and there will be lots of time for conversation and questions. Please, as we're going along, feel free to use the chat.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: To type any comments, any discussion. We have lots of experts here in the room, and that people love to share with one another.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: You can answer one another's questions. If you have a question for Claudius, I would just ask that you use the Q&A button at the bottom of your screen. So, if you, don't see it, just click on More.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And you will see the Q&A button, that's the right place to type your question, or to let us know that you have a question, so that we can help to moderate and organize things as we go.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Claudius, let me pass it to you as more people come in. Welcome, and tell us about what's happening in the city of Hamburg and across cities in Germany.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Yes, welcome, everybody, as well from my side, and thank you very much, Bess, for inviting me to this very interesting course of,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Events, and for the opportunity to…
 
 Claudius Lieven: Report a little about, how we do digital citizen participation.
 
 Claudius Lieven: in Hamburg, Germany, and how we are beginning to use AI to improve and make the participation more impactful.
 
 Claudius Lieven: I would begin to present, to share my presentation.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Okay. Yes, you should be able to. Let's take me off Spotlight and put your slides on.
 
 Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS): Creamy moment.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Thank you. There we go.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Okay, let's begin.
 
 Claudius Lieven: At the start.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Okay.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Yes, I'm going to tell a little about how we move from digital citizen participation to the learning city. I'm Claudius Levin, head of a staff unit for citizen participation in the Ministry of Urban Development and Housing in Hamburg.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Hamburg is one of the 16 federal German states.
 
 Claudius Lieven: I'll go from the where, to the what.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And on to the how we do it.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Firstly, where am I at the moment? I'm in northern Germany, central northern Europe.
 
 Claudius Lieven: about 100 kilometers from the North Sea, in between Amsterdam, Copenhagen, Warsaw, Vienna.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, I'm a hamburger.
 
 Claudius Lieven: But not such one, and we are a lot of hamburgers here, but this is how our city looks, and it is as well circular.
 
 Claudius Lieven: as the hamburgers, but that's the old shape of the defensive wall from the medieval ages. But it's still in the city morphology, and it is a very aquatic city. It's by the River Elbe.
 
 Claudius Lieven: a big stream, and it's a port city, and that's why we are really fond of ships. They can go to the center of the city, right into the harbor. It's 70 square kilometers of harbour in the heart of the city.
 
 Claudius Lieven: But, let's get a bit more serious.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Hamburg is a city republic, and this is a bit of our DNA. Became 1510, a free city in the German Empire, and still we name ourselves the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg. The Hanse was this trade league
 
 Claudius Lieven: Centuries ago. But, it made us become a federal state, a city republic. And,
 
 Claudius Lieven: The State Parliament is, since centuries, called the Burgersaft, which means just citizenry.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And so, it is a self-governing city. We had,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Far-reaching autonomy, over the centuries, aside of these, unfortunate 12 years between 1933 and 45.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Ministerial duties in Hamburg are performed by, currently, 11, senators, who each had, ministry.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Small ministry, of course, in comparison to bigger countries.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, this, Free City tradition, is as well, inscribed in the political system. Of course, it's,
 
 Claudius Lieven: parliamentary republic, and the city parliament is the most important body for political decisions. But we have, as well, the possibility to do referendums, or the citizens have
 
 Claudius Lieven: the possibility to start a campaign which leads to a referendum, and we had just two referendums on the last Sunday.
 
 Claudius Lieven: One was adopted by the majority, the other declined. But that's how it goes, and now we have two decisions, and the city government will enact the referendum that has won.
 
 judith drucker: But…
 
 Claudius Lieven: I am here to talk about another mode that we call the deliberative mode.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, this is about public debate, in, yeah, the,
 
 Claudius Lieven: agora of the city, and our topic especially is the digitization of this public debate, especially in urban development, because my unit is in the Ministry of Urban Development and Housing, and
 
 Claudius Lieven: We advise and support authorities, districts, public companies in participation procedures. We organize information and participation on citywide topics ourself.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And we develop new methods and instruments for citizen participation, and this is especially digital citizen participation.
 
 Claudius Lieven: On the left side, you see our logo and our motto, and that is, in German, auf der Logebauen, or in English, building on dialogue. Because we are very purpose-driven.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Our aim is to further develop the city and to make it possible that a lot of apartments, of housing, can be built.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And that is a thing where citizens have a lot of need to discuss about the changes in their neighborhoods and in the urban environment.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And that is why we developed the DPAS system. DPAS is an acronym for Digital Participation System, and I'll go to explain a little bit how we use that.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Depos consists, broadly spoken, out of 5 elements. The most important is the online participation tool that is quite similar to other online participation tools, like GoVocal, or MapChinaire, or Console.
 
 Claudius Lieven: It is a bit more data-driven.
 
 Claudius Lieven: talk more about that later. And we do, as well, digital participation on-site in events using touch tables and smartphones and combinations of those.
 
 Claudius Lieven: We are connected to our urban data platform, from where we receive all the maps, aerial photos, 3D models, and a lot of other urban data.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And we have specialized evaluation tools.
 
 Claudius Lieven: as well, a point I'll deepen later, and a navigator, which is a KPI dashboard, to give us an overview, as well to give citizens and politicians an overview about what happens in the system and in the debates.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Here you see a screenshot of the navigator. You can easily access this when you Google DPAS Navigator.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, we have carried out more than 130 processes in the last 10 years, and, are, in this year, at about 16 processes. So it's a very continuous,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Work and a debate that is going on.
 
 Claudius Lieven: The online tool?
 
 Claudius Lieven: is map-based in the primary mode. So, citizens give feedback to plans, we present them, and they can comment on the feedback, on the contributions one citizen has written, and they can rate it.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Like, thumbs up, sums down. You can as well do some other things with it, like compare plans and have digital storytelling, but I'll focus here on the map-based participation, because most of the feedback comes through this channel.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, so the question is, solving problems with the public.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, here I have, given an overview about the topics of the processes of 2025.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Because, there you see, we talk a lot with the citizens about concepts, about redesigns, ideas, and as well a little use participation. So it's about how we design the city of the future, how we are continually
 
 Claudius Lieven: developing the city further, redeveloping sites, roads, public spaces, and all this. And this is what is being presented through the system to the citizens, and where we gather feedback, and where we then have to analyze the feedback.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And derive meaningful information, recommendations out of that.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Because in this deliberative pillar of our democratic arena, we do not take decisions. It is about recommendations, it's about debate, and the decisions are taken by the democratically elected bodies.
 
 Claudius Lieven: But the meaningful debate, provides a lot of insight and information about what the citizens want, what they need, maybe about their preoccupations as well, so that we learn where we have to adopt,
 
 Claudius Lieven: But further, precise plans, or to explain more, in detail what is coming.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And this system, the DPAS system, is an open source tool. We have published it on various platforms, and,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Meanwhile, as well, the civil society in Hamburg has adopted it.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And this is a process, here you see on the map, about 2,000, replies, and it is about,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Unsealing the soil.
 
 Claudius Lieven: It means,
 
 Claudius Lieven: You can make suggestions where the pavement should be removed so that more water can enter into the ground.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Why is this important? It is the idea of the sponge city. We live in the time of climate change, and we have to deal with heavy rainfalls, and with flooding within the city.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And one way to prevent that is to unseal, pavement, paved areas. The idea is coming from the Netherlands, there it is very popular. A citizen… a group of citizens' initiatives has adopted the idea
 
 Claudius Lieven: and, implemented a DEPAS system.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, they call themselves Local Power.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And it is now the first time we have a bottom-up initiative in a private-public co-creative process, in cooperation, meanwhile, with the Ministry of Environment. They have said, wow, this is a good idea.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And it is not always a public space, it's… it is, as well, private spaces. So, the driveway to your garage doesn't need to be paved. It can as well be a soil that… a surface that lets water enter in.
 
 Claudius Lieven: So, the URL is here, and so we see that we have not, meanwhile, not only the top-down, because if we offer participation, it is top-down by the government, but it is as well now becoming a bottom-up.
 
 Claudius Lieven: That is something we really like to see, and we encourage that, and hope that more of that is going to happen.
 
 Claudius Lieven: In the next ews.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Another thing is that Dipas is not only used in Hamburg, there are some other German cities who have as well adopted the system. This is a picture of Munich, so a process about the further development of the city center of Munich.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And in Munich, of course, it's not hamburgers, it's pretzels.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And so they, they, changed a little bit the, the icons, that it is a bit more Bavarian.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Just one, Example.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Yes, so, this is, how we apply the digital participation, and we see, the scaling.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And now, last year, it was more than 11,000 contributions, and these contributions often tend to be like letters.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, so it's not just a text, a short text message, but if you think on 11,000 letters, you can imagine that's a whole lot of information.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And,
 
 Claudius Lieven: how do we… how did we achieve this, that the citizens use it so intensively? The first thing is the tool is very easy to use for the citizens. It does not take you much time to write your contribution.
 
 Claudius Lieven: If you do not want to write a thousand characters.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, that helps the citizens to just, provide us their view. An attentive service from my team, who
 
 Claudius Lieven: supports, especially within the administration, the district, planning authorities and the public companies who use it. That is, as well, important to have.
 
 Claudius Lieven: the continuity, Meanwhile, we can say that
 
 Claudius Lieven: For Hamburg, DEPAS is quite well known and learned within the administration, as well as in the public, within the citizens.
 
 Claudius Lieven: been, the most, important thing I, think, I think, is, the trust that, the citizens,
 
 Claudius Lieven: have a few no barrier to use this system. That is because we work very transparent. The source code, of course, is open source.
 
 Claudius Lieven: We work a lot with open data, and we provide everything we know and we can write down as open knowledge, so that everything is understandable and transparent.
 
 Claudius Lieven: On the other hand, the users and the usage of Deepers is anonymous. We do not store any personal data.
 
 Claudius Lieven: That, lowers, the barrier of expressing oneself. But we have no problem with hate speech, I must say. The citizens really use it in a very,
 
 Claudius Lieven: You know, deliberate way, and provide, information.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Communication is important, reporting, presenting, publishing, and working with the stakeholders Initiative Science Foundation, so that trust in this approach grows over the time.
 
 Claudius Lieven: That is, for us, taking the participation promise serious, that we really want to give the citizens a meaningful say in the debate about the…
 
 Claudius Lieven: Development of the city, but…
 
 Claudius Lieven: Taking it serious means working with all the hell lot of information. Just some short view about, a little bit of text, and, it is only text.
 
 Claudius Lieven: But, there is a lot of information within it.
 
 Claudius Lieven: We have the possibility since some years to do statistical analysis. That gives us a very good short overview about quantities of reactions. The green dots mean a lot of people voted sums up to a contribution.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And on the lower right side, you see a line of more reddish dots.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And that is a conflict line. There is one major road where we have problems with the traffic and bicycle lanes and all that, and that expresses directly in the data.
 
 Claudius Lieven: So you can have, really, from, just the, statistics, a quick overview where, the action is highest, and where, maybe conflicts arise, but, here is the…
 
 Claudius Lieven: conflict line, yeah.
 
 Claudius Lieven: But on the other hand, here's another view, we cannot, with this method, read out the text that the citizens provide us. And, of course.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Well, it's just so, 20% of the task solved by doing a statistical analysis, 80% is here in the textual data.
 
 Claudius Lieven: So we began some years ago with the development of an AI-based,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Systems, which helps us to,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Cut through all this, a lot of information.
 
 Claudius Lieven: This has now become an orchestrated, open-source AI pipeline. We use primarily Lama 3.1 and Roberta. It's a BERT derivate, which is specially trained for the German language.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, we have, developed, this,
 
 Claudius Lieven: pipeline, you can see it from top down. It begins with a named entity recognition service. That's for us to eliminate private data. Sometimes people write their names or telephone numbers, and we do not want to have that in our data.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And then it goes on with the key message extraction and so on. I won't go here in details. Later in another session, maybe we can have more of that. But, the core functionalities, are…
 
 Claudius Lieven: The identification of the key messages within the posts, the assignment of these key messages to predefined categories, like mobility, housing, green spaces, or
 
 Claudius Lieven: More, detailed ones.
 
 Claudius Lieven: the aggregation of the messages into aspects, these are
 
 Claudius Lieven: Subclusters, and the aspects then are aggregated into clusters.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Those can be spatially represented, as well the aspects in the clusters, and of course, we still have statistical
 
 Claudius Lieven: Boom.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Information out of the data sets of the contributions.
 
 Claudius Lieven: One example. We have just had in this summer a debate about the remodeling of the train station in the center of Altonard.
 
 Claudius Lieven: This is, one of the Hamburg districts, former independent city, and there, the,
 
 Claudius Lieven: train station shall be relocated, and at the moment, we asked the citizens for comment and feedback for the public spaces surrounding this building you see in the upper right. This is a train station from the early 80s.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, citizens commented, and, road contributions commented, and, rated those, in a plentitude, and if we look on, the statistic at first.
 
 Claudius Lieven: We see that the topic of urban design is that what has received the most response.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, it has, as well, received a lot of ratings, several thousands, and a lot more than all the other,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Categories, which we see here.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And all in all, it's about 3,500 ratings and 400 contributions.
 
 Claudius Lieven: So we ask ourselves, okay, what is in here?
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, yes, this is what we are focusing on.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, so this is a short screen video where I just, entered into, the AI analysis system, to check what is happening in this category of urban design.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, these are all the categories. Now I look on the one with the most contributions. Okay, this is urban design. We have more than 2,300 ratings, positive here, 520 negative.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, 57 aspects. Okay, let's look into these, category. And, to get an overview, we ask for the assessment that citizens… I look for the assessment that citizens gave, and look on the most commented,
 
 Claudius Lieven: contributions, and the AI sums this up together with, okay, we have a
 
 Claudius Lieven: problem with the identity and the centrality of this place. We fear the loss of a historic, building substance.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, we need to better, use the urban potential, of this, area.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Well, so this was for us a moment of aha, because we explicitly asked another question. We asked, give us feedback to the public spaces around the building, but the citizen said, no, we don't want to talk about the building. That is, we thought we can talk about the building later.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Because of the German railway. But, it was, in fact, they said, no, no, we have a problem with this building.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And the learning effect now for us, there the data helped us, and the analysis helped us a lot to inform our senator and those who are steering all the redevelopment process. Now we have to shift our perception about how we can do this planning process.
 
 Claudius Lieven: We need to address the question of the identity and the, question how we…
 
 Claudius Lieven: deal here with… that was what was even before this building. There was a brick-built Neo-Gothic train station, and a lot of people wanted it back. Of course, we will not build that back, but
 
 Claudius Lieven: We will now, in the Urban Design Competition, put a special emphasis on the question of identity and historic connection, so that we, in the best way, take up the citizens' preoccupations. Or not preoccupations, what they desire, what this place should
 
 Claudius Lieven: Due for the center of the district.
 
 Claudius Lieven: You know, this was a very short,
 
 Claudius Lieven: example, how the AI helps us for rapid extraction of key messages out of a participation process, and it allows us to have a transparent, value neutral, and traceable
 
 Claudius Lieven: Analysis, and this enables well-founded conclusions and recommendations to those who are steering the urban development in our city.
 
 Claudius Lieven: This increases the impact of the participation.
 
 Claudius Lieven: what we try and what we want to achieve. What we see in the same moment is that the use of AI in evaluating citizen contributions requires sensitive communication, because if we just say we use AI, we need to explain some things, and this system is absolutely
 
 Claudius Lieven: open source, it's transparent, and we are going to publish everything of it. And that is, we think, very important, to maintain the trust of the citizens. On the strategic level, we…
 
 Claudius Lieven: are looking forward to, that we have the possibility to uptake geo-referenced local knowledge at scale, because we have tens of thousands of contributions, and we'll collect more.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, we can make it a persistent knowledge layer in our urban digital twin. So, not just to analyze a single process, but groups of processes, topics, and to
 
 Claudius Lieven: Analyze the, debate over time, and how topics and, conflicts develop.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Yes, this… We hope.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Leads us to,
 
 Claudius Lieven: The possibility to become more or less a learning city, to have a feedback loop, a better feedback loop from what the citizens, think and perceive how the urban development is carried out, and, so that we have a…
 
 Claudius Lieven: Solid base to, be closer to the demands and the needs of the citizens in how we are
 
 Claudius Lieven: Carrying out the urban development.
 
 Claudius Lieven: So far, For the first, presentation, and, I'll…
 
 Claudius Lieven: Stop the screen share, and we are open for the… Discussion.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Claudius, thank you so much. That was really wonderful. What I want to do is, to start by just asking you some clarifying questions. There are many questions that have come in in the chat that are, let me call it clarifications.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And encourage people in the meantime to put more reflective questions in the Q&A so that we know, we want to talk. While I'm asking questions, we'll keep the recording going. As is our practice, once we open it up for conversation, we will turn off the recording so that people can feel free to ask
 
 Beth S. Noveck: anything and everything. So a whole bunch of clarifying questions. The first one is, do all projects get mapped and used with DPUS, or how do you select which projects?
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Should I give you one at a time, or would you like all of them? Or three of them?
 
 Claudius Lieven: Okay, 3 is a good bump. I'll give you 3.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So the first is about how you select a project, or is it all projects? Second clarifying question is, you said it's anonymous, but is registration required?
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And then there was a third question about, sort of, the length
 
 Beth S. Noveck: and phases of a project. Is there a standard cadence for how long a project lasts… sort of an engagement lasts? Does it have phases, or does it vary from project to project? Let me stop there.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Okay. And then we'll do one more round. And again, please put further questions in the Q&A so we can open it up.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Yes, the question, if all projects are mapped.
 
 Claudius Lieven: All projects that are carried out with DPAS are mapped, because it's a map-based system, but it's not all participation projects of Hamburg. We are doing participation in urban development, and there are, as well, other participation processes run by
 
 Claudius Lieven: the Department of Social Affairs, or, Sometimes from the,
 
 Claudius Lieven: the Education Ministry, they have, as well, participation processes, which are mostly not map-based. So, most things in…
 
 Claudius Lieven: the urban space, around mobility, around green spaces, around urban design that is carried out with DPAS, and it is, and that is important, the informal
 
 Claudius Lieven: participation. We have, as well, formal participation, which is obliged by law. That is working a little bit different.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Has, as well, a digital, prong, but, That is not…
 
 Claudius Lieven: that transparent and not that easy to use. There you have a registration necessity, and with DPAS, you have no registration necessity. Our philosophy is to work really with a low barrier.
 
 Claudius Lieven: The system is as well digitally barrier-free, according to our standards in Germany, so that you can use it as well with a screen reader. It's not so easy with a map, of course. Maps are quite hard to make them barrier-free, but this is as well an aspect.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And the anonymity, of course, has advantages and disadvantages. One advantage is we can share the data easily within the administration. Otherwise, if it be mixed with private data, that would be much more
 
 Claudius Lieven: Difficult, and it has this low barrier regarding presenting yourself.
 
 Claudius Lieven: On the other hand, of course, we often would know, would like to know more about, our customers, or who has said what, which age groups, from where do the people come, and so on.
 
 Claudius Lieven: We can integrate questionnaires into the system, where we, as well, do not directly collect personal data, but things like,
 
 Claudius Lieven: highest education, zip code, age group, gender, and all these things. So, to get a bit of socio-demographic overview about who has taken part in the participation.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Yes, and, the… the processes, we…
 
 Claudius Lieven: In general, advise, to do not only digital participation, but to have a mix of on-site events.
 
 Claudius Lieven: at least, information event at the beginning, or some, as well, workshops, if possible. And,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Then, accompanying the, online participation.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And within the planning process,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Usually, the online participation is opened around 4 weeks, sometimes shorter, sometimes a little longer, but in the planning process, when we want to get to a redesigned plan, we usually calculate it should take us
 
 Claudius Lieven: half a year to a year, and so you cannot open the commenting phase for a year. You need to have, like, 4 weeks, and usually we see, as well, in the
 
 Claudius Lieven: Pattern, that in the first days, the reaction is more intense, and then it goes down, and after 4 weeks, it's very little that then comes.
 
 Claudius Lieven: So it's… that is how it is embedded into the planning process.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And the, one more clarifying question, which is how many staff does it take now, versus previously? But I think there's a, there's a staffing question. What does it take to do this?
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Practically.
 
 Claudius Lieven: Yes. I have in my unit two colleagues who just do, the, attentive service. So, who are, advising, districts, public companies, how to carry it out. They carry it out themselves, they are the local administrators.
 
 Claudius Lieven: They have, as well.
 
 Claudius Lieven: To do, the evaluation afterwards.
 
 Claudius Lieven: And, in the,
 
 Claudius Lieven: local authorities, it is the, the colleagues, there is no, no dedicated personnel for that.
 
 Claudius Lieven: There's… it's the planners, the urban planners, usually, who do it, often supported, by,
 
 Claudius Lieven: Specialized, bureaus, planning, agencies who, who support them, but,
 
 Claudius Lieven: So we cannot directly say, okay, we reduced the stuff broadly, but we can say, and we can see we increased the activity broadly. So we have a lot more participation processes than we had 10 years ago in this forum.
 
 Claudius Lieven: So with the same personnel, we, see it… there can, a lot more be done than before.
 
 judith drucker: Hmm.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So we have so many questions waiting, and I have such a cold that I am going to open it up to others to ask their questions. I'm putting the queue in the chat. Again, if you can mute yourselves so we don't hear you in the background, but I'm going to invite.
